title: Pad Thai
subtitle: stir-fried rice noodles with prawns, egg, and tamarind sauce
excerpt: Pad Thai is Thailand's most famous noodle dish. Flat rice noodles are stir-fried with prawns, egg, and a tangy tamarind-fish sauce dressing. It is best cooked in small batches over very high heat so the noodles fry rather than steam.
sourceNotes: Pad Thai was promoted by the Thai government in the 1930s and 40s as a way to encourage rice noodle consumption during a rice shortage. It combined Chinese stir-fry technique with Thai flavours. From a government-sponsored dish, it became one of the world's most recognised Thai exports.

content.text: Pad Thai is best cooked over the highest heat your hob can produce. A wide frying pan works if you do not have a wok -- but cook in two batches rather than one to avoid steaming the noodles. Soak the noodles ahead of time so they are ready when you need them.

items.prepNote: use 200g flat rice noodles -- soak in warm water for 20 minutes until pliable, then drain
use 100g bean sprouts -- or shredded cabbage
use 2 tbsp tamarind paste -- or lime juice

content.text: Make the sauce: mix the fish sauce, tamarind paste (or lime juice), honey, and chilli flakes in a small bowl.
Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a wok or wide frying pan over the highest heat possible. Add the prawns. Stir-fry for 2 minutes until pink. Remove and set aside.
Add the drained noodles to the hot pan. Toss for 1 to 2 minutes. If they stick, add a splash of water.
Push the noodles to the side. Add 1 tablespoon of oil to the centre. Crack in the eggs and scramble quickly. Toss together with the noodles.
Return the prawns. Pour over the sauce. Add the spring onion and bean sprouts. Toss everything for 1 to 2 minutes.
Serve with lime wedges and extra chilli flakes.

items.symptom: Noodles are sticking together in clumps
items.cause: Noodles too wet or pan not hot enough
items.fix: Drain the soaked noodles well and pat dry. Make sure the pan is smoking hot before adding the noodles. Toss constantly and add small splashes of water if needed -- not too much.

content.text: Pad Thai is eaten everywhere in Thailand -- from street carts to restaurants. The combination of sour, sweet, salty, and spicy is the blueprint of Thai flavour. Street versions are cooked in giant woks over fierce gas burners. The key to replicating this at home is very high heat and small batches.
